Reading the Capability Map

A Handbook for the Capability Gap Radar — Need vs. Achievement, and its Model Implications for Industrial Strategy

Author

Net Zero Industrial Policy Lab (NZIPL) · Johns Hopkins SAIS

Published

July 8, 2026

What this is. A working handbook for reading the model-driven Capability Gap Radar of the Atlas of the Clean Industrial Base — and its finer companion, the PC Scatter — and turning them into industrial-strategy calls. It explains the one idea both panels encode (a gap between what a technology needs and what a country has achieved), the seven-cell grid that names every gap, and a worked example for each cell drawn from live model output (a recent three-year window, six focal countries). The method behind the two axes is documented in capability_radar_methodology.qmd; this note is the reader’s guide to using them.

1 How to use this handbook

Read §2–3 once to learn the framework, then treat §4 as a reference: each of the seven cells has a plain-language meaning, a reading rule, a policy orientation, and a real worked case. §5 walks a full country read end to end. §6 covers what the map does not say — the limits matter as much as the signal.

The framework is deliberately coarse. It classifies clusters of capability, not individual products. As the underlying working paper puts it: precision beyond the cluster level “would be applying a false level of precision to the model.” The handbook is a guide to reasoning, not a recipe.

2 The two questions behind every panel

Both panels answer two questions at once and plot one against the other.

What does the technology need? — the winners’-recipe target. The competitiveness model (a Random Forest predicting whether a country reaches RCA > 1 in a clean technology) tells us which capabilities carry the predictive signal. But we do not read its importances naively: we take the model’s signed SHAP contributions and average them over only the country-years where a producer is actually competitive — the winners. Summing those to five capability clusters — Chemicals, Electronics, Industrial Materials, Machinery, Metals — gives a target share \(t_c\) (% of the winners’ recipe) for each cluster. High share = a capability competitive producers genuinely lean on. Crucially this is magnitude-weighted, not a count of HS codes, and direction-checked (see target_profile.qmd), so it names the cluster that matters, not merely the one with the most products.

What has the country achieved? — the achievement fraction. For each cluster we take the country’s own recent competitive-class signed SHAP and divide it by that cluster’s target weight. The result, the achievement fraction \(a_c\), is what the country has ÷ what the technology needs: \(a_c \geq 1\) means the country sits at the winners’ frontier, \(a_c \to 0\) means the capability is essentially absent. Because the numerator is the country’s own signal, achievement carries all the country-specific information — the frontier is shared, the achievement is unique.

Panel Need Achievement / Have Granularity
Capability Radar dashed frontier, 5 axes (winners’ recipe) green fill, 5 axes (achievement fraction) Category (5 clusters)
PC Scatter x-axis (product SHAP importance) y-axis product RCA (bubble = trade value) Product (HS6)

The radar and the scatter are the same comparison at two zoom levels. The radar reads each cluster’s achievement against its need; the scatter shows the individual products inside a cluster. This distinction is not cosmetic — it is the single most common source of misreading (§4.1).

3 The gap framework: a seven-cell grid

Crossing three need levels with three achievement levels yields a 3×3 grid that collapses to seven policy-relevant cells.

Need level (what the technology requires — winners’-recipe target share)

Level Threshold Meaning
Core \(t_c \geq 30\%\) A cluster competitive producers genuinely lean on — usually one or two per tech, running 30–76%
Supporting \(10\% \leq t_c < 30\%\) A real but secondary requirement
Peripheral \(t_c < 10\%\) The technology barely draws on this cluster

Achievement level (what the country holds, relative to that need)

Level Threshold Meaning
At frontier \(a_c \geq 1.0\) Already at the winners’ level (\(\gg 1\) = surplus)
Partial \(0.5 \leq a_c < 1.0\) Meaningfully building, still below the frontier
Behind \(a_c < 0.5\) Little or none of the required capability yet

The grid

At frontier \(a\geq1\) Partial \(0.5\leq a<1\) Behind \(a<0.5\)
Core need \(\geq30\%\) 🟢 Leverage 🟠 Build-up 🔴 Critical gap
Supporting 10–30% 🟡 Mature strength 🟠 Build-up 🟥 Gap
Peripheral \(<10\%\) 🔵 Bonus strength ⚪ Not a priority ⚪ Not a priority

The diagonal logic is the whole point: the top-left is where a country’s achievement meets the technology’s core need (act here first), and the top-right is where the technology’s most important need is unmet (the hardest, most strategic problem).

4 The seven cells, with worked examples

Each cell below pairs the reading rule with a real case from model output. The recurring cases — India · Solar, Brazil · Biofuel, Mexico · Heat Pumps — reappear because a single country×technology typically spans several cells across its five clusters. That is normal and is exactly how the map is meant to be read.

4.1 A note before the cells: radar vs. scatter

Brazil · Biofuel — capability radar (category level)
Cluster Need % Achievement Classification
Chemicals 40.7 53% Build-up
Machinery 30.4 70% Build-up
Industrial Materials 26.6 69% Build-up
Metals 2.3 0% Not a priority
Electronics 0.0 0% Not a priority

On the radar, Brazil · Biofuel shows no Leverage cell — its core and supporting clusters (Chemicals, Machinery, Industrial Materials) all sit in Build-up, meaningfully built but not yet at the frontier. Yet on the PC scatter, Brazil holds clear leverage products: sugarcane-derived ethanol and processing inputs where its product-level RCA is far above 1 and the model weights the product heavily. Both readings are correct. The category average dilutes a handful of star products; the scatter resolves them. Rule: use the radar to set the strategic frame, the scatter to find the specific products to anchor.

4.2 🟢 Leverage — achievement meets core need

Reading rule: Core need (\(\geq30\%\)) and achievement \(\geq 1\). The country already sits at the frontier in the capability the technology most demands.

Policy orientation: Anchor FDI and supply-chain strategy here. This is the nucleus to build outward from — the country competes where it counts. A large surplus (\(a_c \gg 1\)) is spare capacity to redeploy.

Worked case — Mexico · Heat Pumps.

Mexico · Heat Pumps — capability radar (category level)
Cluster Need % Achievement Classification
Machinery 75.9 138% Leverage
Metals 12.9 94% Build-up
Electronics 7.3 164% Bonus strength
Industrial Materials 2.2 216% Bonus strength
Chemicals 1.7 118% Bonus strength

Machinery is the overwhelming core need of heat pumps (the winners’ recipe is machinery-dominated), and Mexico sits at or beyond that frontier — the textbook leverage position: the country is strong exactly where the technology is decided.

4.3 🟠 Build-up — close enough to matter

Reading rule: Core or Supporting need and Partial achievement (\(0.5 \leq a < 1\)). The country is just below the frontier in a capability that matters.

Policy orientation: Highest expected return on targeted investment. A modest push to reach \(a_c = 1\) converts a near-miss into a genuine strength. Expect an import surge in the relevant capital goods before the export signal follows.

Worked case — Brazil · Biofuel (above). All three of Brazil’s non-trivial biofuel clusters sit in Build-up — Chemicals, Machinery and Industrial Materials each at roughly half to two-thirds of the frontier. This is a country one coordinated push from competitiveness across the capabilities biofuel most rewards, consistent with its established ethanol complex.

4.4 🔴 Critical gap — the top driver is missing

Reading rule: Core need (\(\geq30\%\)) and Behind (\(a < 0.5\)). The model’s single most important capability is absent.

Policy orientation: The hardest problem. Requires upstream industrial policy — sector-building, not just incentives. Cannot be closed by demand subsidies alone.

Worked case — India · Solar.

India · Solar — capability radar (category level)
Cluster Need % Achievement Classification
Electronics 61.6 17% Critical gap
Chemicals 23.3 81% Build-up
Metals 8.4 101% Bonus strength
Machinery 6.1 259% Bonus strength
Industrial Materials 0.5 4% Not a priority

India assembles modules competitively, but the winners’ recipe for solar is dominated by Electronics (≈62% of the target) — the cell/inverter power-electronics layer — and India is barely a fifth of the way to that frontier. That is the critical gap: strong at the visible end of the chain, absent where the model says competitiveness is actually decided. (Note this is not Chemicals: measured by magnitude rather than product count, Electronics is Solar’s true core — see §5.)

4.5 🟡 Mature strength — real but not decisive

Reading rule: Supporting need (10–30%) and achievement \(\geq 1\). A genuine capability at the frontier, in a cluster of secondary importance.

Policy orientation: Maintain and deepen. Useful, but not enough on its own to carry a technology strategy.

Worked case — Japan · Magnets. The Machinery cluster (need 21%, achievement 211%) is a maintained specialisation that supports, but does not by itself decide, competitiveness in this technology.

4.6 🟥 Gap — a secondary driver missing

Reading rule: Supporting need (10–30%) and Behind (\(a < 0.5\)). An important-but-not-critical capability is absent.

Policy orientation: Worth addressing, but not a show-stopper alone. Sequence it after the critical gaps.

Worked case — India · Biofuel. The Industrial Materials cluster is a supporting need (27%) the country has barely built (achievement 0%) — a real but second-order weakness to address once the core gaps are underway.

4.7 🔵 Bonus strength — strength the tech doesn’t reward

Reading rule: Peripheral need (\(<10\%\)) and achievement \(\geq 1\). A frontier (often surplus) capability in a cluster this technology weights lightly.

Policy orientation: Do not anchor tech-specific strategy here — but flag it: this strength may be decisive for a different technology. A cross-technology asset.

Worked case — India · Geothermal. A frontier Industrial Materials position (achievement 265%) that the Geothermal recipe weights only 1% — real capability, but better leveraged for a technology that prizes it.

4.8 ⚪ Not a priority — neither side cares

Reading rule: Peripheral need and Partial/Behind achievement. Neither the technology nor the country emphasises this cluster.

Policy orientation: Low-salience. Note and move on — strategy capacity is better spent on the actionable cells above.

Worked case — India · Solar · Industrial Materials. Trivial model need (≈1% of the winners’ recipe) and near-zero Indian achievement: correctly ignored in a solar strategy.

5 The worked cases, as radars

The five cases above, drawn as capability gap radars. On each, the dashed pentagon is the winners’ frontier (100% of the need) and the green fill is the country’s achievement fraction per cluster; each axis is labelled with its achievement (values above 100% are surpluses, drawn clipped to the ring). The axis-label colour is the seven-cell class (key in the sixth panel) — this is what carries the need magnitude, so a low green vertex reads very differently under a red Critical gap label than under a grey Not a priority one. Reading the shape together with the colour: a green vertex reaching the ring under a green/red label sits on a cluster the technology needs; one collapsing toward the centre under a red label is the strategic gap.

Reading the five together: Mexico · Heat Pumps fills its core Machinery axis to the ring (green Leverage label); Brazil · Biofuel sits part-way out on its three needs (orange Build-up labels across the board); India · Solar is full on Machinery/Metals — but those wear blue Bonus strength labels, while the near-empty Electronics axis wears the red Critical gap one; Japan · Magnets overshoots Machinery under a Mature strength label; and India · Biofuel shows the feedstock-processing shape thinned toward the centre, its Industrial Materials axis a Gap.

6 A full read: India · Solar, end to end

Read top to bottom by need: Electronics is the top driver and a Critical gap (the strategic priority — India reaches only ≈17% of the frontier). Chemicals is a supporting need India has largely met — a Build-up to finish. Metals and Machinery are at or beyond the frontier but peripheral for solar — Bonus strength, real capability that matters more for other technologies (magnets, wind) than for solar. Industrial Materials is Not a priority. One panel, a complete sequencing of where to act and in what order — and, notably, it points Indian solar policy at electronics sector-building, not the chemicals layer a product-count reading would have flagged.

7 What the map does not say

  • Clusters, not products. A core-need cluster signals what kind of capability matters, not a list of HS6 codes to build. Use the scatter to descend to products, but treat product specifics as illustration, not prescription.
  • Radar dilutes; scatter resolves. A Build-up cluster can hide a leverage product (and vice versa). Always cross-check the two panels (§4.1).
  • Macro features are excluded. The model also learns from FDI, trade openness, GDP and other country covariates; the need is built over the five traded-capability clusters only. A country can have a clean radar yet face non-trade barriers.
  • Achievement is a recent, revealed signal. The achievement fraction reads the country’s own competitive-class contribution over a recent three-year window — it reflects capability the country has revealed, not nascent capacity. Pair with the trade-timeline and firm-activity panels for momentum.
  • The frontier is shared, not local. The need is the winners’ recipe, identical for every country by design; a country very unlike the typical winner still gets measured against the same frontier. That is the intended reading of “a standard profile countries evolve toward,” but it means the map answers what to build toward, not the only path there.
  • Thresholds are conventions. The 30% / 10% and 1.0 / 0.5 lines are defensible but not magic. Cases near a line should be read as “between cells,” not snapped to one.

8 One-page cheat sheet

Cell Need (target share) Achievement Do
Leverage Core At frontier Anchor FDI; build outward
Build-up Core/Supporting Partial Invest — highest return; reach the frontier
Critical gap Core Behind Sector-build upstream; hardest problem
Mature strength Supporting At frontier Maintain and deepen
Gap Supporting Behind Address after critical gaps
Bonus strength Peripheral At frontier Don’t anchor here; asset for another tech
Not a priority Peripheral Partial/Behind Note and move on

Radar = category zoom (set the frame). Scatter = product zoom (find the anchor). Need = winners’-recipe target share; achievement = country’s signed SHAP ÷ that need, recent three-year window.
